I found some statistics that might illustrate my point. One country has a bit over 15 million voters. In a recent federal election, one major party received 33.38%, another major party got 32.02%, a smaller party received 4.29%, a green party got 8.65%, and all other parties combined received 21.66% (this figure was inflated due to confusion with another party). I realize that this is based on a traditional media environment, but that's how any system would have to start as well.

Using those numbers - $30 per voter, 15 million voters, and the percentage of the vote - you can estimate how party funding might have looked after the last election.

Major Party 1 - $150,210,000.  
Major Party 2 - $144,090,000.  
Green Party - $38,925,000.  
Other parties - $97,470,000, but this amount must be divided among various smaller parties and independents, resulting in very small individual amounts. A legitimately small party, for example, that received 0.61% would have received approximately $2.75 million.

You're not allowed to donate to parties privately, right? Those funds must sustain the parties for three years, not just cover advertising in the weeks leading up to the election. If you estimate that 75% of the funding goes to renting offices, overheads, and advertising, then 25% is allocated for staff salaries. The small party would receive about $680,000. Dividing that by three for the years, it comes down to roughly $225,000. That could potentially pay for about four staff members at $56,000 per year. How many seats did they run for again?

So, a couple of reasons, and something to say first:

Before I get into it, mecha isn't really a sensible genre label. It's more like an aesthetic. Mecha shows are usually sci-fi, or drama, or thriller, or action, just like other shows. So if you dislike, say, a particular action/science fiction series, you could go watch a war drama instead, then try an action/music crossover, maybe check out a theatrical thriller, or a character drama/eldritch horror. Hell, some people (like certain online databases) call a surrealist comedy a mecha, so you could check out that insane show too.

Anyway, what's appealing about the mecha tropes? Heaps of stuff. Here's a few: There's a lot of complex technical animation that accompanies the huge robots. They're sometimes rendered in great detail, which is impressive to see. So there's the visual aspect.

Another is the scale of the things - they go between the size of cars, to the size of buildings, to, in rare instances, the size of the observable universe (thanks to a well-known animation studio!). That's the sort of thing you don't normally see, so someone might get hooked on that.

I mean, there's the whole action side of things, too. What good's a giant mecha if it's not gonna blow some stuff up? This means we get to see weapons on a scale that's uncommon outside of mecha, we get to see choreography that doesn't make sense on the ground or for normal people, and mecha can be destroyed but the pilot can live, so defeat is a little more common in mecha narratives I guess?

They also have their own set of aesthetic design tropes (distinct from tropes that are common in mecha shows). So, like, if you get why people might be interested in muscle cars, or motorcycles, or tanks, or military jets, or that new luxury fashion range, or that particular architect, or that famous painter... well, it's the same. There's lots of depth to the visual design, and plenty of people learn to love that. This is possibly my favourite reason: I've learned that mecha just *look awesome*.

tl;dr all sorts of reasons. It's an aesthetic that shows up in lots of different genres that are attractive for their own reasons.

This systematic lowering of expectations may be a greater long-term danger than its immediate fruits. The placeholder currently occupying a significant political position – the latest in a sequence stretching back over a long decade – is a living reminder of how difficult it is to draw a bead on a government’s short-term failures when they have no discernible long-term projects in mind.

Everywhere, there is a sense that no one can imagine any higher task for government than managing an eternal present. As a major natural wonder is pitilessly bleached to the colour of dead bones, a regional government has been bending over backwards to accommodate a massive new coal mine.

The inevitable consequences of fostering a dirty and retrograde industry, and the long slide in its price, are never allowed to intrude on the present. That’s because our politics seems incapable, for now, of imagining any future that differs, for good or ill, from whatever is given.

If the centre of our politics is such a moral and intellectual vacuum, we can’t be surprised when all kinds of detritus washes in from the fringes. A candidate from a fringe party who believes that the world’s media fakes refugee photos is, in any case, not so jarring alongside the waving through of inquiries into food practices, or the presumption of guilt that underpins the bipartisan commitment to keeping refugees in offshore facilities.

They’re all artefacts of drift, of an absence of principle and imagination. Of something that may never manifest itself as a catastrophe, but instead as a steady and remorseless unwinding. A slow leak that can only be patched with belief.
